Borrow, then personalize

How I tried to predict a new person’s brain responses from a few hundred images, and what I learned on the way

EEG
fMRI
brain encoding
transfer learning
A walkthrough of my EEG and fMRI project: a big shared network lost to a simple average of other people, and a small personal map on top of that average became the main result.
Published

November 6, 2026

← All posts

Code and protocols on GitHub

The question

When you look at a picture, your brain answers with a pattern. We can record it with EEG (sensors on the head) or with fMRI (a scanner). An encoding model takes the image and predicts this pattern. It does not look at the pixels directly: a ready-made image network first turns each photo into a list of numbers (its features), and the encoding model learns how these numbers relate to the brain response. In the main tests the features come from AlexNet, the image network used by the THINGS-EEG2 authors.

A good model for one person needs many hours of their recordings. A new person usually gives much less, maybe a few hundred labelled images. But we already have models of many other people. So my question was simple:

If I have only a few hundred images from a new person, what is the best way to use them, when models of other people already exist?

I did this work on free Kaggle notebooks. I had no GPU of my own, so every idea had to be cheap enough to run there.

First, what the data looks like

Everything later in this post is easier if you know what one piece of data is. So let me show it first.

In all five datasets the setup is similar. A person sits and looks at many photos of objects and scenes, one after another, while a machine records their brain. Each photo gives one brain response. One photo together with this person’s response to it is what I call a labelled image. A model learns from these pairs.

🖼️
1. A photo A cat, a banana, a street… Thousands of different photos, some of them shown many times.
→
🧠
2. A recording EEG: a cap of sensors on the head measures fast electrical signals. fMRI: a scanner measures slow changes of blood flow in small spots of the brain.
→
📈
3. A response EEG: 17 sensors at the back of the head, above the visual part of the brain (out of the 64 in a lab cap), and 100 time points in one second: one every 10 milliseconds (ms). fMRI: one number for each of tens of thousands of brain spots.

These are the five datasets I used. Three are EEG and two are fMRI. The first number on each card is how many people I tested as “new people”.

THINGS-EEG1
EEG · lab
  • 24 new people
  • 64-sensor lab cap
  • Photos flash quickly; training photos recorded once
  • Up to about 22,000 labelled images per person
THINGS-EEG2
EEG · lab
  • 10 people
  • 64-sensor lab cap
  • 16,540 training photos, each shown 4 times
  • 200 test photos, each shown 80 times. Why? One recording is mostly noise; the average of 80 shows the brain's real answer.
  • Up to 16,540 labelled images per person
Alljoined-1.6M
EEG · consumer
  • 16 people
  • 32-sensor consumer headset, cheaper and noisier
  • Same photo set as THINGS-EEG2
NSD
fMRI · 7 tesla
  • 8 people
  • Very strong scanner, very clean data
  • Up to 3 repeats per photo, averaged
  • About 8,000 to 9,000 labelled images per person
NOD
fMRI · 3 tesla
  • 21 new people
  • Common hospital-strength scanner
  • Each photo recorded only once
  • 800 labelled images per person

I can’t show the real photos here, because their licences don’t allow it. But one dataset, THINGS-EEG2, shares its recordings openly, so Figure 1, Figure 2 and Figure 3 use real EEG. I took the test part of the data (the 200 test photos with their 80 repeats, see the THINGS-EEG2 card above) for all 10 people, and made small averages from it on Kaggle.

A real response. Figure 1 shows the signal of one sensor at the back of the head (Oz, above the visual cortex) for five photos. Time 0 is the moment the photo appears. In this dataset the photos come very fast, a new one every 200 ms, so the line is never flat: you also see the waves of the photos before and after, and that makes the regular ripple. The response to this photo is where the five coloured lines split apart, most clearly in the grey band, 100 to 200 ms. That early response is what I scored in the EEG tests. Pick another person from the menu: the general shape stays, but the details move.

One photo, 80 times. The five coloured lines in Figure 1 are averages over 80 recordings each. A single recording is very noisy. In Figure 2 each thin grey line is one of the 80 repeats: one time that this person saw the cat photo, and the thick green line is their average. You can almost not see the response in a single line, but the average shows it clearly. Keep this in mind: later it explains why the method works on some datasets and not on others.

Are two people similar? This is the key question for the whole project. If two people answer the same photos in the same way, we can borrow from one to predict the other. Here is how I measured it, step by step:

  1. One person’s pattern. For one person, take the response to each of the 200 test photos: 17 sensors × 100 time points per photo. So the pattern is a big table of numbers that says how this person answered every photo.
  2. Keep only what is special about each photo. All photos share a common wave (the dashed grey line in Figure 1). I subtract it, so what is left is how each photo is different from the others. That is the part an encoding model must predict.
  3. Two halves. I split the 80 repeats into two halves: repeats 1 to 40 and repeats 41 to 80. Each half gives its own pattern, made from different recordings, so each half has its own noise.
  4. Compare with a correlation. 1 means the two patterns are the same, 0 means they have nothing in common.
    • Same person: first half against second half of the same person. This is the best we can hope for, because even one person does not match themself perfectly: the noise is different in each half.
    • Two people: the first half of one person against the second half of another person. I use halves here too, so both comparisons have the same amount of noise and are fair to each other.

Figure 3 shows all these comparisons. The row is the person of the first half, the column the person of the second half. The squares on the diagonal compare a person with themself; all other squares compare two people.

In Figure 3, the squares on the diagonal are darker than the rest. On average, two halves of the same person are similar at 0.39, and two different people at 0.15. This is not zero: people respond to the same photos in a similar way. That is why borrowing from other people works at all. But it is clearly lower than the same person: each person also has their own part. That is the part a personal map should learn.

The idea in one (made-up) picture. Figure 4 is not real data. It is a small made-up example of a brain map, to show the idea of the project before the real results. Each person’s response is a shared part, plus a personal part, plus noise. If you average many other people, their personal parts cancel out and the shared part stays: this is borrowing. What is left between borrowing and the person is what the personal map must learn from that person’s few labelled images. Pick a person from the menu.

With this picture in mind, the rest of the post is the story of how I found that borrowing is a strong start, and that a small personal map on top of it helps when the person’s labelled images are clean enough.

The path, in one picture

  1. IdeaOne big shared network for all people, with a small part for each person.
  2. Reproduce firstA published EEG model and its baselines, number by number.
  3. Looks goodThe shared network wins on the ten people I built it with.
  4. The real testWritten down first, run once on 24 new people. It loses to a simple average.
  5. BorrowAverage the models of other people. No labels needed.
  6. PersonalizeA small linear map on top, learned from a few hundred images.
  7. Test againNew people on consumer EEG and two kinds of fMRI, and a repeat on THINGS-EEG2.
  8. WhyThe map needs room to improve and clean labels.

Where I started: a big shared network

At the start I followed the trend in the field. Many recent papers train one network on many people and add a small part for each person. My plan was the same: one shared network for everyone, and a small extra part trained for each new person.

Before building anything, I reproduced a published EEG encoding model and its baselines (the simple standard models that every new method must beat, such as a linear model from the image features to the response), and checked that my numbers matched the paper. This step was slow and boring, but later it saved me. Every new idea was compared with baselines that I knew were correct.

On THINGS-EEG2 (ten people) the shared network looked good. With 250 or 500 images from a new person it beat the baselines. I was happy. But there was a problem: I had used these same ten people while building the model. A model can look good on the people it was tuned on. Work like this, where I can look at the data and try things, is what I call development. It is useful for finding ideas, but it does not prove them.

The test that changed the project

So I wrote the test down before running it. A protocol is a short file where I wrote, before the run, what I would measure and which result would count as a success. I saved it in git, so the order (protocol first, results later) is on record. It fixed the model, the people, the score, and the margin: the smallest gain I agreed to call real, and not luck. Then I ran the test once, on 24 people of a second EEG dataset (THINGS-EEG1) that no model had seen. A test written down like this before the run is called prespecified.

The score is encoding accuracy, written r: the correlation between the predicted response and the real one, in the early response (100 to 200 ms, the grey band in Figure 1). 1 would be perfect, 0 means no relation. EEG is noisy, so real values are small, around 0.1 to 0.2.

The shared network beat the person’s own model: a model trained only on the person’s own few hundred labelled images (250 or 500; the charts show the average of the two). But it lost to something much simpler: just average the predictions of the models of other people. I call this borrowing. The test said “rejected”, and I kept that result.

In Figure 5, use the menu above the chart to switch between the two comparisons. Each line is one person. A coloured line means the method on the right was better for this person; a grey line means the method on the left was better. Hover a point to see the person.

In Figure 5, borrowing was better than the person’s own model for 22 of 24 people. The shared network was below borrowing for 18 of 24.

This was the most important moment of the project. I had spent a lot of time on the big network, and a plain average of other people beat it, on people it had never seen. If I had not written the test first, I could have searched for some setting where the network wins, and I would have believed it.

Borrow, then personalize

So I changed the direction. If borrowing is such a strong start, the new person’s few hundred images should not build a model from zero. They should correct the borrowed prediction.

The correction is small on purpose. It is a linear map that mixes the borrowed prediction across EEG sensors (or fMRI brain spots) in the way this one person needs. It is kept small (regularised), so it cannot learn too much from a few hundred images. I call it the personal map. Two steps:

  1. Borrow. Average the predictions of models trained on other people. No labels of the new person needed. This works because everyone’s data is in the same layout: the same 17 sensor positions for EEG, and the same template brain surface for fMRI, so “brain spot number 1,000” is the same place in every person.
  2. Personalize. Fit the small map from the new person’s labelled images, on top of that average.

Then I did the same as before: protocol first, one run, a fixed margin. On the 24 THINGS-EEG1 people the map improved on borrowing for 23 of them, in the early response. To be honest about it: this follow-up used the same 24 people as the first test, and I wrote it after I saw the first result, so it is weaker evidence than a test on fresh people.

Does it hold on other data?

One dataset is not enough. So I wrote new protocols and tested the same idea on new people in three more datasets: a consumer EEG headset, 7-tesla fMRI and single-trial 3-tesla fMRI (each photo recorded only once, with no repeats to average, like one thin grey line in Figure 2). I also repeated the test on THINGS-EEG2, on the ten people I had used before. Each test was run once.

In Figure 6 every dot is one person. Above zero means the map was better than borrowing for that person. The red dashed line is the margin that the protocol said a gain must clear. Next to the dots, the grey mark shows the average gain, and its bar shows the range where the true average very likely is (made a bit wider because each test compares several things at once). A test passes when the whole bar is above the margin. Hover a dot for the person, or the grey mark for the numbers.

What Figure 6 says, in short:

  • Lab EEG (THINGS-EEG1 and THINGS-EEG2): the map helped, for almost every person. On THINGS-EEG2 the map beat borrowing by more than the margin, which is what Figure 6 shows. But the protocol also asked it to beat two other methods by the margin, and against one of them it fell a little short. So the THINGS-EEG2 test as a whole is “not sure”. Its people were also the ones I used to build the baselines, so it is the weaker of the two.
  • Consumer EEG (Alljoined, 16 people): the gain went the same way, for 12 of 16 people, but did not clear the margin. The answer here is “not sure”, and I report it like that.
  • 7-tesla fMRI (NSD, 8 people): the map helped every person. Encoding accuracy went from 0.25 with borrowing to about 0.30 with the map, about a fifth higher.
  • Single-trial 3-tesla fMRI (NOD, 21 people): no gain. And this was the result I had predicted in the protocol, before the test. The next section says why.

Why it works sometimes and not always

The pattern became clear from the development work (exploring the data, not prespecified tests). The map can only fix what borrowing leaves on the table. It needs two things:

  1. Room. Noise puts a ceiling on any score. Even a person’s own two halves agree only so much (the diagonal of Figure 3). If borrowing is already close to that ceiling, there is nothing left to gain.
  2. Clean labels. The map learns from the new person’s responses. If each response is very noisy, the map learns noise.

NOD records each image only once, on a 3-tesla scanner, so its labels are very noisy. That is why I predicted no gain there, and the test agreed.

The clean-label part I could check directly on THINGS-EEG2, where each image was shown several times. I trained the map on labels that averaged 1, 2 or 4 repetitions, and kept everything else the same. There are two kinds of map. The full map can mix every sensor with every other sensor. The low-rank map is a smaller version that only works along the 200 main directions of the borrowed prediction; it is the one I used for fMRI, where there are too many brain spots for a full map. In Figure 7, use the menu above the chart to switch between the two maps and two label budgets (how many labelled images the person gives: 250 or 500).

Figure 7 shows that with cleaner labels the gain grows, for the same people and the same number of images. So the few hundred images of a new person are worth more when each one is recorded well.

Encoding is not the same as identifying

In fMRI I also looked at a second task, identification: given a brain response, which of 200 images was the person looking at? The model predicts a response for each of the 200 images, and we check if the closest prediction belongs to the right image. A model can be good at predicting responses and still be less good at picking the image, so I scored both. In the main fMRI test (NSD), the map combined with the person’s own model picked the right image 7.4 percentage points more often than borrowing, for all 8 people.

Figure 8 follows the same people while they give more and more labelled images, up to their whole recording. It uses features from DINOv2, a newer and stronger image network than the AlexNet of the main test, so all numbers are higher. Click a name in the legend to hide or show it. Each thin line is one person.

In Figure 8, with 500 images the map on borrowing is far ahead of the person’s own model. With more images the own model catches up, but even with the whole recording the map stays a little ahead, and adding the own model to it helps a bit more. Borrowing matters most when you have little data from the person, and it does not hurt when you have a lot.

What I take from it

  • Write the test before you run it. My first idea failed its test. Without the protocol I would have kept the wrong story.
  • Try the simple thing first. A plain average of other people was stronger than the network I spent so long on.
  • Reproduce before you improve. Correct baselines made every later comparison clear.
  • Small and cheap can be enough. All of this ran on free Kaggle notebooks. The final method is a few lines of linear algebra.
  • Say “not sure” when the data says “not sure”. The consumer EEG result is inconclusive, and it stays like that.

Limits

The EEG gains are small, a few hundredths in correlation. Each test that passed rests on one dataset, and no result has been repeated yet on a second group of fresh people. Some tests reused people that I had seen before (the follow-up on THINGS-EEG1 and the repeat on THINGS-EEG2), and I say this in each place. The parts about room, label noise and identification are development analyses, not prespecified tests.

Where to look

Everything is on GitHub: the code, the protocols of every test, the commit that holds each protocol before its run, and the result tables behind every figure. The charts on this page are built from those tables with a short script (data/prepare_data.py in this post’s source folder). The real EEG examples come from the openly shared THINGS-EEG2 recordings (Gifford et al., 2022, CC-BY 4.0), averaged by a small Kaggle script (data/kaggle_eeg_examples/ in the same folder).
